items.title: Rolling back a failed release
items.passage: # Rolling back a failed release **Applies to:** Container Service, Functions ## Symptoms - A release has introduced errors and must be reverted - The previous revision is needed while a fix is prepared ## Common causes - A defect reached production that testing did not catch - A configuration change had unintended effects ## Resolution

items.title: Rolling back a failed release
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Open the revisions page for the service and identify the last revision that was healthy. 2. Select roll back on that revision. Traffic moves within roughly thirty seconds and no rebuild takes place. 3. If the release included a database migration, roll the migration back before the service, or the older code will encounter a schema it does not expect. 4. Record the incident and the reason for the rollback before deploying a fix, while the detail is still fresh. ## Notes Rollback restores the container image and its configuration together. It does not restore data.

items.title: Build failures caused by dependency resolution
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Pin your dependencies with exact versions and commit the lock file. Unpinned dependencies are the cause in the large majority of cases of this kind. 2. Compare the runtime version declared in your build configuration against the version you use locally. 3. Clear the build cache from the settings page and trigger a fresh build to rule out a corrupted artefact. 4. If a specific dependency is failing to resolve, check whether its registry is reachable from the build network. ## Notes Build logs retain the full resolution output for thirty days, which is usually enough to identify which version changed.

items.title: Responding to a suspected account compromise
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Revoke all API keys for the affected account immediately. This is disruptive and it is the correct first action. 2. Force a password reset and terminate active sessions for the affected users from the team members page. 3. Review the audit log for the period in question, filtering by the affected user, and record anything unexpected before it ages out. 4. Enable multi-factor authentication for all users if it is not already mandatory for the organisation. ## Notes Audit logs are retained for ninety days on Business plans and one year on Enterprise. Export them promptly during an investigation.

items.title: Multi-factor authentication setup and recovery
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Ask the user to check that automatic time synchronisation is enabled on the device generating the code. Drift is the most common cause by a wide margin. 2. If the device is lost, the user should sign in with one of their recovery codes and then re-enrol a new device from the security page. 3. Where no recovery codes are available, an account administrator can reset multi-factor authentication for that user from the team members page. 4. If the user is the sole administrator and has no recovery codes, identity verification through support is required and takes up to one business day. ## Notes Support cannot disable multi-factor authentication without identity verification, regardless of urgency.

result.answer:
Hi there,

To ensure your secrets do not appear in the logs, you should store them as secrets rather than standard environment variables. Secrets are masked in logs and are not readable through the API after creation [DOC-DEPLOY-004]. 

Since your secrets are currently being printed at startup, please treat them as exposed and rotate them immediately, even if your logs are private [DOC-DEPLOY-004]. To do this, first revoke the exposed credentials, then issue replacements with the narrowest scope that still works [DOC-SEC-002]. You should also search your audit log for any use of the exposed credentials from unfamiliar addresses during the time they were visible [DOC-SEC-002]. 

After updating your configuration, remember to redeploy your service, as running containers will not pick up new values without a restart [DOC-DEPLOY-004].

Best regards,
Support Team
result.answer_reason: The documentation explicitly states that secrets should be stored as secrets to be masked in logs and provides a clear resolution path for exposed credentials, including rotation and audit log checks.

result.answer:
Hi there,

I'm sorry to hear you are having trouble accessing the console. Since your colleague is able to sign in successfully, it is likely an issue specific to your account or device rather than a general outage.

Please try the following steps to resolve the MFA rejection:

1. Check your device's time settings: Ensure that automatic time synchronization is enabled on the device generating your MFA code. Clock drift of more than thirty seconds is the most common cause of invalid codes [DOC-AUTH-002].
2. Verify the authenticator enrollment: Confirm that your authenticator app is enrolled against the correct account [DOC-AUTH-002].
3. Check for account lockout: If you have made multiple failed attempts, your account may be locked. Check the security page of the console for a red banner indicating a lock; this usually unlocks automatically after thirty minutes [DOC-AUTH-001].
4. Clear browser data: Try clearing cookies for the CloudServe domain or using a private browsing window to rule out stale session issues [DOC-AUTH-001].

If these steps do not resolve the issue and you have lost access to your authenticator device, you can sign in using one of your recovery codes and re-enroll a new device from the security page [DOC-AUTH-002]. If you do not have recovery codes, an account administrator can reset your MFA from the team members page [DOC-AUTH-002].

Please let me know if you are still unable to access your account after trying these steps.

Best regards,
Support Team
result.answer_reason: The documentation provides specific troubleshooting steps for MFA rejections (clock drift, wrong account) and general login issues (account lockout, stale cookies) that directly address the user's symptoms.

1. **Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) URL:** Ensure the ACS URL in your identity provider matches the value shown on the SSO settings page exactly, including the trailing path [DOC-AUTH-003].

items.title: Responding to a suspected account compromise
items.passage: # Responding to a suspected account compromise **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - Unrecognised activity appears in the audit log - A user reports credentials may have been exposed - Resources were created that nobody claims ## Common causes - Credentials were reused from a service that suffered a breach - An API key was committed to a public repository - A former team member retained access after leaving ## Resolution

items.title: Managing team members, roles and permissions
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Check the effective permissions view for the user, which resolves direct roles and group memberships together. 2. Confirm the invitation was accepted. Pending invitations appear in a separate section and expire after seven days. 3. Remove a departing user rather than only changing their password, and revoke any API keys they created. 4. Prefer group membership to direct role assignment, so that access can be reviewed in one place. ## Notes Removing the last account owner is not permitted. Transfer ownership before removing the account.

items.title: API key rotation and scope management
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Check the API keys page for the key's status and expiry. Revoked and expired keys are listed with the date and the user who acted. 2. Review the scopes attached to the key. Read-only keys cannot write, and project-scoped keys cannot reach organisation endpoints. 3. To rotate without downtime, create the replacement key first, deploy it, confirm traffic has moved, then revoke the old key. 4. If a key has been exposed publicly, revoke it immediately rather than waiting for the rotation window. ## Notes Keys issued to individual users are removed when that user is deleted. Use service accounts for anything running in production.

items.title: API key rotation and scope management
items.passage: # API key rotation and scope management **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - A previously working key returns 401 Unauthorized - A key works for some endpoints and not others - A key needs replacing after accidental exposure ## Common causes - The key was revoked or reached its configured expiry - The key was issued with a scope that excludes the endpoint being called - The key belongs to a deleted user and was removed with the account ## Resolution

items.title: Handling exposed secrets and credential rotation
items.passage: # Handling exposed secrets and credential rotation **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - A key has been committed to a repository - A secret appears in application logs - A third party has reported finding a credential ## Common causes - Configuration was committed rather than referenced from the environment - The application prints its configuration during startup - A key was shared in a support ticket or a chat message ## Resolution

items.title: Connecting continuous integration pipelines
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Create a service account for the pipeline rather than using a personal key, so that access survives staff changes. 2. Grant the service account only the projects and permissions the pipeline needs, and review that grant when the pipeline changes. 3. Store the credential as an encrypted secret in your pipeline provider, never in the repository. 4. Test the pipeline credential separately from the deployment logic, so that authentication failures are distinguishable from deployment failures. ## Notes Service account keys do not expire by default. Set an expiry and rotate on a schedule.

items.title: Handling exposed secrets and credential rotation
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Revoke the exposed credential first. Removing it from the repository does not help, because it remains in the history. 2. Issue a replacement with the narrowest scope that still works, rather than recreating the original permissions by default. 3. Search the audit log for use of the exposed credential from unfamiliar addresses during the exposure window. 4. Add secret scanning to your pipeline so that the next occurrence is caught before it reaches a remote branch. ## Notes Never send a live credential to support. Support will never ask for one, and any credential shared in a ticket must be treated as exposed.
